findings.statement: The investment firm is a financial entity within the scope of DORA and must comply with DORA's ICT risk management, digital operational resilience and ICT incident reporting requirements.

Within DORA, the cloud provider qualifies as an ICT third-party service provider and the cyberattack constitutes an ICT-related incident that the firm must assess against the definition of a major ICT-related incident.

The firm's management body must define, approve and oversee the implementation of the firm's ICT risk management framework and bears ultimate responsibility for ICT risk, including the risk arising from the cloud-hosted AI system integrated into its trading infrastructure.
The firm must identify and document its ICT-supported critical or important functions, including its trading function, and the ICT services and ICT third-party providers supporting them.
The firm must implement backup policies, disaster recovery plans and restoration and recovery procedures enabling it to recover the trading systems that were disrupted for more than a day.

The firm must handle the cyberattack through a documented ICT-related incident management process that detects, manages and notifies incidents, and must classify the incident in accordance with the harmonised classification criteria.

Given the disruption of its critical trading systems for more than a day, the firm must determine whether the incident is major and, where it is classified as major, report it to its competent authority: an initial notification within 4 hours after classification and in any case no later than 24 hours after becoming aware, an intermediate report within 72 hours, and a final report within one month.
Where the incident is classified as major under DORA, the firm must inform its clients of the incident and of the measures adopted to mitigate its adverse effects.

In relying on the cloud provider for its trading function, the firm retains full responsibility for compliance with DORA, must pre-assess the provider and its ICT services, and its arrangements with the provider must contain the key contractual provisions, including access and audit rights, cooperation duties and exit strategies.

The firm's reliance on a single cloud provider for a function supporting its critical trading infrastructure requires a documented and updated preliminary assessment of the ICT concentration risk arising from that dependence.
The firm is the controller of the client personal data processed by the AI system, and the cloud provider, which hosts and processes that data on the firm's behalf, is a processor.

The cloud provider's processing of client personal data on the firm's behalf must be governed by a contract meeting Article 28(3), covering the subject-matter and duration of the processing, security measures and assistance with breach obligations.

The firm must maintain appropriate technical and organisational security measures for the client personal data, including the ability to restore the availability of and access to that data in a timely manner in the event of the technical incident that occurred.

The firm must notify the competent supervisory authority of the suspected personal data breach without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of the clients concerned.
As the firm's processor, the cloud provider must notify the firm without undue delay after becoming aware of the suspected unauthorised access to the client personal data.

Where the suspected unauthorised access to client information is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of the affected clients, the firm must communicate the personal data breach to those clients without undue delay.

Because the traders make the investment decisions using the system's recommendations, the decisions are not based solely on automated processing, so the GDPR regime for solely automated decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects is not triggered on these facts.
The firm acts as a deployer of the AI system because it uses the system under its authority in the course of its investment business.

As a deployer of the AI system, the firm must take measures to ensure, to its best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy among its staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of the system, including the traders who rely on its recommendations.

The investment recommendation system does not fall within any of the AI use cases listed in Annex III on the facts stated and is therefore not a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2), so the deployer obligations for high-risk AI systems do not automatically apply to the firm.

The same event triggers parallel obligations under separate regimes: a report of the major ICT-related incident to the firm's competent financial authority under DORA and, separately, a personal data breach notification to the supervisory authority under the GDPR, each with its own deadlines and recipients.

summaries.relevance: Brings the investment firm within DORA's scope as a financial entity, which is the gateway for every DORA conclusion in this answer.

Supplies the definitions used to characterise the cloud provider as an ICT third-party service provider and the cyberattack as an ICT-related incident, framing the incident-management and third-party findings.
Places responsibility for ICT risk management on the firm's management body, anchoring the governance dimension of the firm's dependence on the cloud-hosted AI system.
Requires the firm to map its critical trading function and the ICT third-party services supporting it, which is how the cloud provider's role is brought under DORA's management requirements.
Grounds the obligation to restore the disrupted trading systems through backup, disaster recovery and restoration procedures after the more-than-one-day outage.
Supports the duty to inform clients about the major ICT-related incident, complementing the GDPR communication duty owed to the same clients.
Requires the documented incident-management process through which the firm must handle the cyberattack and feed the classification and reporting steps.
Sets the harmonised criteria that decide whether the disruption of critical trading systems is a major ICT-related incident, which gates the reporting conclusion.

Carries the core incident-reporting conclusion: the deadlines and procedure for reporting a major ICT-related incident to the competent authority are the central DORA obligation in this scenario and also support the parallel-regimes finding.
Establishes that the firm retains full responsibility and must pre-assess the cloud provider, forming the backbone of the third-party-dependence analysis.
Requires the documented preliminary assessment of ICT concentration risk arising from reliance on a single cloud provider for the trading function.
Defines the contractual content (access, audit rights, cooperation, exit) that the firm's arrangements with the cloud provider must secure, directly relevant to its dependence on that provider.
Defines the firm as controller, the status on which all of the firm's GDPR duties for the client personal data rest.
Defines the cloud provider as processor, which allocates the breach-notification duty towards the firm to the provider rather than to the firm.
Defines the solely-automated-decision threshold that the scenario's human-in-the-loop use does not meet, narrowing the data-protection analysis of the recommendation outputs.
Requires the processor contract governing the cloud provider's processing of client data in the course of hosting the AI system.
Grounds the security and timely-restoration duty for the client personal data implicated by the attack and the outage, a central data-protection obligation in the scenario.
Sets the 72-hour notification duty to the supervisory authority, the core data-protection obligation triggered by the suspected unauthorised access, and supports the parallel-regimes finding.
Obliges the cloud processor to notify the firm without undue delay of the breach it discovered, shaping the division of incident duties between the parties.
Triggers communication to the affected clients where the suspected access is likely to result in high risk, paralleling DORA's client-information duty for the same audience.
Defines the firm as deployer of the AI system, the status from which its AI Act duties flow.
Imposes the AI-literacy duty on deployers, the principal AI Act obligation applying to the firm for the recommendation system as used by its traders.
Makes Annex III systems high-risk, so its non-engagement on these facts explains why the high-risk deployer obligations do not automatically apply.
Lists the high-risk use cases against which the recommendation system's classification is settled; its non-engagement is what keeps the system outside the high-risk regime.

actions: Verify the AI system's actual functionality against the AI Act's Annex III categories, since the conclusion that the high-risk regime does not apply rests on the system not matching any listed use case.

Establish which entity developed and supplies the AI system and on what terms the cloud provider hosts it, in order to settle provider and deployer roles under the AI Act and processor status under the GDPR.

Examine the firm's arrangements with the cloud provider to confirm whether they constitute an Article 28 GDPR processing contract and contain the DORA Article 30 key contractual provisions, including audit and exit rights.

Settle whether the suspected unauthorised access amounts to a personal data breach and where it falls on the GDPR Article 33(1) risk and Article 34(1) high-risk thresholds, having regard to the client data actually involved.
Confirm whether the more-than-one-day disruption of the trading function meets the DORA Article 15 criteria for classification as a major ICT-related incident for Article 19 reporting purposes.
